candidate.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication administration and client education, pp. 38-40.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — inhaled corticosteroid teaching
candidate.educational_objective: Teach clients using inhaled fluticasone to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after each inhaled dose to reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis risk.

options.A: Use fluticasone only when acute wheezing begins because inhaled corticosteroids are intended to provide rapid bronchodilation during an asthma attack.
options.B: Swallow water immediately after each dose so medication remaining in the mouth is carried into the stomach and continues the anti-inflammatory effect.
options.C: Rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after each inhaled dose to help reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis.
options.D: Avoid any valved holding chamber because spacers increase oral drug deposition and therefore increase the risk of candidiasis during inhaled corticosteroid treatment.

candidate.rationale: Current fluticasone propionate inhalation-aerosol labeling directs patients to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhalation to help reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis. It is maintenance therapy and is not indicated for acute bronchospasm. A misuses it as rescue therapy, B incorrectly tells the client to swallow the rinse, and D contradicts the label, which permits a valved holding chamber in appropriate patients.
candidate.source_claim_supported: After inhalation, rinse the mouth with water without swallowing to reduce oropharyngeal candidiasis; fluticasone is not rescue treatment for acute bronchospasm; a valved holding chamber may be used in appropriate patients.
